claim: Taste responses in the rodent gustatory cortex (GC) progress through firing-rate epochs that culminate in the emergence of action-related firing.
source: Taste responses in the rodent gustatory cortex (GC) span this sensorimotor divide, progressing through firing-rate epochs that culminate in the emergence of action-related firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The emergence of action-related firing is a sudden, coherent and variably-timed ensemble transition.
source: Population analyses reveal this emergence to be a sudden, coherent and variably-timed ensemble transition that reliably precedes gaping onset by 0.2–0.3s.
evidence: This is supported by population analysis methods described in the manuscript and references to prior studies.

claim: The action-related ensemble transition reliably precedes gaping onset by 0.2–0.3s.
source: Population analyses reveal this emergence to be a sudden, coherent and variably-timed ensemble transition that reliably precedes gaping onset by 0.2–0.3s.
evidence: This temporal relationship is demonstrated through the experimental data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 0.5s GC perturbations significantly delayed gaping when they preceded the action-related transition.
source: Perturbations significantly delayed gaping, but only when they preceded the action-related transition - thus, the same perturbation impacted behavior or not, depending on the transition latency in that particular trial.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding, supported by the behavioral data presented in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: The same perturbation impacted behavior or not, depending on the transition latency in that particular trial.
source: Perturbations significantly delayed gaping, but only when they preceded the action-related transition - thus, the same perturbation impacted behavior or not, depending on the transition latency in that particular trial.
evidence: This trial-specific effect is demonstrated through change-point analysis and behavioral measurements.

claim: The results suggest a distributed attractor network model of taste processing.
source: Our results suggest a distributed attractor network model of taste processing, and a dynamical role for cortex in driving motor behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and theoretical considerations discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Cortex has a dynamical role in driving motor behavior.
source: Our results suggest a distributed attractor network model of taste processing, and a dynamical role for cortex in driving motor behavior.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the timing-dependent effects of cortical perturbations on behavior.

claim: Animals must decide to either swallow or expel the sensory stimulus in the mouth when tasting.
source: The gustatory system is an ideal model to study this proposed coupling, because animals necessarily respond to tastes with discriminative behaviors - specifically, they must decide to either swallow or expel the sensory stimulus in the mouth (Grill and Norgren, 1978a; Katz and Sadacca, 2011; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: GC neurons respond to taste presentation with a sequence of firing-rate 'epochs'.
source: GC neurons respond to taste presentation with a sequence of firing-rate 'epochs', two of which are taste-specific: neural firing first carries information regarding the physio-chemical identity of the taste stimulus, and then correlates with palatability, a variable intimately linked with the animal's decision to ingest or expel the taste (Katz et al., 2001; Fontanini and Katz, 2006; Grossman et al., 2008; Piette et al., 2012; Sadacca et al., 2012; Maffei et al., 2012; Jezzini et al., 2013; see also Crouzet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: Neural firing first carries information regarding the physio-chemical identity of the taste stimulus.
source: GC neurons respond to taste presentation with a sequence of firing-rate 'epochs', two of which are taste-specific: neural firing first carries information regarding the physio-chemical identity of the taste stimulus, and then correlates with palatability, a variable intimately linked with the animal's decision to ingest or expel the taste (Katz et al., 2001; Fontanini and Katz, 2006; Grossman et al., 2008; Piette et al., 2012; Sadacca et al., 2012; Maffei et al., 2012; Jezzini et al., 2013; see also Crouzet et al., 2015).
evidence: This temporal sequence is supported by cited prior work and the data in this manuscript.

claim: Neural firing then correlates with palatability, a variable intimately linked with the animal's decision to ingest or expel the taste.
source: GC neurons respond to taste presentation with a sequence of firing-rate 'epochs', two of which are taste-specific: neural firing first carries information regarding the physio-chemical identity of the taste stimulus, and then correlates with palatability, a variable intimately linked with the animal's decision to ingest or expel the taste (Katz et al., 2001; Fontanini and Katz, 2006; Grossman et al., 2008; Piette et al., 2012; Sadacca et al., 2012; Maffei et al., 2012; Jezzini et al., 2013; see also Crouzet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and the palatability analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The transition between identity and palatability epochs happens suddenly and coherently within neural ensembles.
source: Ensemble analyses further reveal that the transition between these two epochs happens suddenly and coherently within neural ensembles (Jones et al., 2007; Sadacca et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior ensemble analysis studies.

claim: The ensemble transition to palatability coding is highly variable in latency (between 0.5 and 1.5s post stimulus, depending on the trial).
source: This ensemble transition to palatability coding, though highly variable in latency (between 0.5 and 1.5s post stimulus, depending on the trial), is a strong predictor of the onset of the animal's consumption-related orofacial behavior (Sadacca et al., 2016), even when the timing of this behavior is manipulated by learning (Moran and Katz, 2014) or cueing (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This variability is documented in cited prior work and demonstrated in the change-point analysis in this manuscript.

claim: The ensemble transition to palatability coding is a strong predictor of the onset of the animal's consumption-related orofacial behavior.
source: This ensemble transition to palatability coding, though highly variable in latency (between 0.5 and 1.5s post stimulus, depending on the trial), is a strong predictor of the onset of the animal's consumption-related orofacial behavior (Sadacca et al., 2016), even when the timing of this behavior is manipulated by learning (Moran and Katz, 2014) or cueing (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This predictive relationship is supported by citations and the behavioral analysis in this manuscript.

claim: The ensemble transition predicts behavior even when the timing of this behavior is manipulated by learning.
source: This ensemble transition to palatability coding, though highly variable in latency (between 0.5 and 1.5s post stimulus, depending on the trial), is a strong predictor of the onset of the animal's consumption-related orofacial behavior (Sadacca et al., 2016), even when the timing of this behavior is manipulated by learning (Moran and Katz, 2014) or cueing (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior learning study.

claim: The ensemble transition predicts behavior even when the timing of this behavior is manipulated by cueing.
source: This ensemble transition to palatability coding, though highly variable in latency (between 0.5 and 1.5s post stimulus, depending on the trial), is a strong predictor of the onset of the animal's consumption-related orofacial behavior (Sadacca et al., 2016), even when the timing of this behavior is manipulated by learning (Moran and Katz, 2014) or cueing (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior cueing study.

claim: GC neural ensembles appear to 'hop' from one attractor state to another during taste processing.
source: That is, GC neural ensembles appear to 'hop' from one attractor state to another during taste processing (Miller and Katz, 2010; Miller, 2016), with the hop representing the reaching of a consumption decision - and (potentially) the emission of a motor signal to brainstem circuits that generate orofacial behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited theoretical work and the experimental findings.

claim: The hop between attractor states represents the reaching of a consumption decision.
source: That is, GC neural ensembles appear to 'hop' from one attractor state to another during taste processing (Miller and Katz, 2010; Miller, 2016), with the hop representing the reaching of a consumption decision - and (potentially) the emission of a motor signal to brainstem circuits that generate orofacial behavior.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by the timing relationship between neural transitions and behavior.

claim: The hop between attractor states potentially represents the emission of a motor signal to brainstem circuits that generate orofacial behavior.
source: That is, GC neural ensembles appear to 'hop' from one attractor state to another during taste processing (Miller and Katz, 2010; Miller, 2016), with the hop representing the reaching of a consumption decision - and (potentially) the emission of a motor signal to brainstem circuits that generate orofacial behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Optogenetic perturbation of the entire GC taste response significantly changes the probability of rejection behaviors in response to aversive tastes.
source: This prediction recently received indirect support when it was shown that optogenetic perturbation of the entire GC taste response (Li et al., 2016) significantly (if modestly) changes the probability of rejection behaviors in response to aversive tastes ('gapes'; Grill and Norgren, 1978a; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior optogenetic study.

claim: 244 GC single neurons were recorded across 10 sessions of 0.5s perturbations.
source: We recorded the activity of 244 GC single neurons across 10 sessions (24.4 ± 13 units/session) of 0.5s perturbations, and of an additional 73 GC single neurons in five sessions (14.6 ± 4.7 units/session) of 2.5s perturbations.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data collected.

claim: 73 GC single neurons were recorded in five sessions of 2.5s perturbations.
source: We recorded the activity of 244 GC single neurons across 10 sessions (24.4 ± 13 units/session) of 0.5s perturbations, and of an additional 73 GC single neurons in five sessions (14.6 ± 4.7 units/session) of 2.5s perturbations.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data collected.

claim: The AAV-ArchT construct used in this study infects neurons of multiple types in an unbiased manner.
source: The AAV-ArchT construct used in this study has been shown to infect neurons of multiple types (e.g., pyramidal neurons and interneurons) in an unbiased manner (Aschauer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior characterization study.

claim: The firing of 60% of GC neurons (146/244) was significantly suppressed during 0.5s perturbations.
source: This expectation was borne out in the data: the firing of most of our GC neural sample (146/244, 60%, example shown in Figure 2A1–A4) was significantly suppressed during 0.5s perturbations, but the firing of an additional 20% (49/244) was significantly enhanced.
evidence: This is directly measured from the neural recordings during optogenetic perturbation, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The firing of 20% of GC neurons (49/244) was significantly enhanced during 0.5s perturbations.
source: This expectation was borne out in the data: the firing of most of our GC neural sample (146/244, 60%, example shown in Figure 2A1–A4) was significantly suppressed during 0.5s perturbations, but the firing of an additional 20% (49/244) was significantly enhanced.
evidence: This is directly measured from the neural recordings during optogenetic perturbation, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: 82% of GC neurons (60/73) were inhibited during 2.5s perturbations.
source: The same pattern of results was observed with 2.5s perturbations: the firing of 82% of GC neurons (60/73, example unit in Figure 2B1–B2) was inhibited, and the activity of 15% (11/73) was enhanced.
evidence: This is directly measured from the neural recordings during optogenetic perturbation, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: 15% of GC neurons (11/73) showed enhanced activity during 2.5s perturbations.
source: The same pattern of results was observed with 2.5s perturbations: the firing of 82% of GC neurons (60/73, example unit in Figure 2B1–B2) was inhibited, and the activity of 15% (11/73) was enhanced.
evidence: This is directly measured from the neural recordings during optogenetic perturbation, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Early and middle 0.5s perturbations delay the peak of palatability firing by approximately 0.5s.
source: Early and middle 0.5s perturbations delay the peak of palatability firing by ∼0.5s; the magnitude of this peak, however, is the smallest for the middle perturbation.
evidence: This is shown in the palatability analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: Gapes occur in 4–6Hz bouts.
source: However, the variability in the amplitudes and durations of these EMG bursts reduces our ability to separate gapes from other large mouth movements. We therefore made use of a more robustly distinctive feature of gaping – the fact that gapes occur in 4–6Hz bouts (Travers and Norgren, 1986; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior EMG studies.

claim: On average, gaping begins approximately 0.9s after Qui delivery in control trials during the 0.5s perturbation sessions.
source: On average, gaping begins ∼0.9s after Qui delivery in control trials during the 0.5s perturbation sessions – that is, when analysis is restricted to trials in which GC neurons were not perturbed (Figure 5A, inset).
evidence: This is measured from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 5A inset.

claim: Neither infection nor implantation affect the ability to gape to Qui.
source: Furthermore, this estimate matches up with observations in control rats (published in Sadacca et al., 2016 and Li et al., 2016) that received neither laser nor ArchT expression. Thus we can conclude that, at least with regard to the driving of gaping, our preparation leaves the system capable of normal function – neither infection nor implantation themselves affect the ability to gape to Qui.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with cited control data.

claim: GC perturbation fails to disrupt ongoing bouts of gaping.
source: Furthermore, these late 0.5s perturbations failed to prematurely end gaping bouts that had already begun. Figure 5B1–B4 show example trials in which the probability of gaping rhythm in the EMG signal went high following Conc Qui delivery, and stayed high throughout late 0.5s perturbations.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the example trials shown in Figure 5B1-B4.

claim: The percentage of trials in which gaping was maintained into the late perturbation period was unchanged by late 0.5s perturbation.
source: In fact, the percentage of trials in which gaping was maintained into this period was unchanged by late 0.5s perturbation - 57% (36/63) of control trials vs 55% (26/47) of perturbed trials.
evidence: This is a direct comparison of trial percentages from the behavioral data.

claim: GC is of no consequence for the maintenance of ongoing gaping.
source: We can thus conclude that GC is of no consequence for the maintenance of ongoing gaping.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of late perturbations on ongoing gaping.

claim: Early 0.5s perturbations delayed gaping onset by approximately 0.25s on average.
source: In contrast, GC activity plays a clear role in the initiation of gaping: early 0.5s perturbations – that is, those delivered well before transitions into the palatability-related state of GC activity – delayed gaping onset by approximately 0.25s on average (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: Middle 0.5s perturbations of GC delayed the onset of gaping until just before 1.2s after taste administration.
source: Similarly, middle 0.5s perturbations of GC delayed the onset of gaping until just before 1.2s after taste administration - approximately 0.25s after gaping on no-laser trials.
evidence: This is measured from the behavioral analysis.

claim: 0.5s perturbations of GC activity occurring either before or during the 'heart' of quinine processing had a strong impact on the latency of aversive orofacial behavior.
source: That is, 0.5s perturbations of GC activity occurring either before or during the 'heart' of quinine processing had a strong impact on the latency of aversive orofacial behavior.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral effects shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 2.5s perturbations delayed the appearance of gaping by approximately 0.2s.
source: Not only is the impact of this brief optogenetic perturbation significant, it was every bit as large as that observed with whole-trial (i.e., 2.5s) perturbations, which delayed the appearance of gaping by ~0.2s (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: The neural transition can potentially happen at any of a range of latencies spanning the approximate interval between 0.5 to 1.5s.
source: Previous demonstrations that the temporal dynamics of GC taste responses are well described in terms of sudden transitions between stimulus-specific ensemble firing rate 'states' (Jones et al., 2007; Sadacca et al., 2016) also reveal large trial-to-trial variability of both the behavioral and neural transition latencies. These studies show that the neural transition can potentially happen at any of a range of latencies spanning the approximate interval between 0.5 to 1.5s, and that orofacial behavior follows close behind, such that trial averaging smears the changes in firing rates into a more gradual-seeming ramp.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and the change-point analysis in this manuscript.

claim: Orofacial behavior follows close behind the neural transition.
source: These studies show that the neural transition can potentially happen at any of a range of latencies spanning the approximate interval between 0.5 to 1.5s, and that orofacial behavior follows close behind, such that trial averaging smears the changes in firing rates into a more gradual-seeming ramp.
evidence: This temporal relationship is supported by citations and the data in this manuscript.

claim: Transitions into palatability-related activity occurred prior to perturbation in 55% of the analyzed middle 0.5s perturbation trials (92/168).
source: Transitions into palatability-related activity (CP) occurred prior to perturbation in 55% of the analyzed trials (92/168).
evidence: This is measured from the change-point analysis of middle 0.5s perturbation trials.

claim: On trials in which the ensemble transition occurred prior to the perturbation, significant palatability-related information appeared in single neuron firing.
source: Regression analysis revealed that, on average, significant palatability-related information appeared in single neuron firing during trials in which the ensemble state transition occurred prior to the perturbation; this information was notably lacking in trials in which the transition had not occurred by perturbation onset (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in the regression analysis in Figure 7B.

claim: On trials in which the ensemble transition had not occurred by perturbation onset, palatability-related information was notably lacking in single neuron firing.
source: Regression analysis revealed that, on average, significant palatability-related information appeared in single neuron firing during trials in which the ensemble state transition occurred prior to the perturbation; this information was notably lacking in trials in which the transition had not occurred by perturbation onset (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in the regression analysis in Figure 7B.

claim: On trials in which middle 0.5s perturbation arrived before the ensemble transition, the delay in gaping was far larger (more than approximately 0.5s).
source: Next, we applied the outcome of this analysis to the behavioral data (Figure 7C): overall, middle 0.5s perturbations delayed gaping by ∼0.25s (data reprinted from Figure 5A); on trials in which that perturbation arrived before the ensemble transition, however, the delay in gaping was far larger (more than ∼0.5s) - on these trials, gaping onset was delayed until more than 0.2s after the end of the perturbations.
evidence: This is shown in the trial-specific behavioral analysis in Figure 7C.

claim: When middle 0.5s perturbation was restricted to trials in which CP happened at 0.65s or earlier, the onset of gaping was not delayed.
source: When we restricted our analysis to middle 0.5 perturbation trials in which CP happened at 0.65s or earlier (that is, prior to perturbation onset, see above), meanwhile, the onset of gaping was not delayed.
evidence: This is measured from the trial-specific behavioral analysis.

claim: Gaping on trials where CP occurred early (0.65s or earlier) occurred more than 300ms earlier than in control trials.
source: In fact, gaping on these trials occurred more than 300ms earlier than in control trials – the predictable result for trials in which the neural process of reaching a decision to gape completed early.
evidence: This is measured from the trial-specific behavioral analysis.

claim: Once the decision to gape has been made, 0.5s perturbations have no impact on the execution of the decision.
source: These data demonstrate that, once this decision (which clearly involves this GC activity, see above and Sadacca et al., 2016) has been made, 0.5s perturbations have no impact on the execution of the decision.
evidence: This is inferred from the trial-specific behavioral analysis showing no delay when perturbations occur after the transition.

claim: In a few late 0.5s perturbation trials (20/168, 12%), the perturbation arrived before CP.
source: Change-point analysis revealed this to be the case: in a few (20/168, 12%) of the late 0.5s perturbation trials, the perturbation arrived before CP.
evidence: This is measured from the change-point analysis of late 0.5s perturbation trials.

claim: When late 0.5s perturbation trials in which the perturbation arrived before CP were removed from the analysis, 95% of the difference between the gaping latency in late 0.5s perturbation trials and control trials vanished.
source: When these trials were removed from the analysis, 95% of the difference between the gaping latency in late 0.5s perturbation trials and control trials vanished.
evidence: This is measured from the trial-specific behavioral analysis.

claim: The impact of brief optogenetic perturbation of GC activity depends both on when that perturbation occurs and on precisely what state the brain has achieved prior to that perturbation.
source: As a whole, our results demonstrate that the impact of brief optogenetic perturbation of GC activity depends both on when that perturbation occurs and on precisely what state the brain has achieved prior to that perturbation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the trial-specific analysis of perturbation effects.

claim: The onset of palatability-related population activity in GC marks a discrete shift in taste processing.
source: This result provides support for our overarching hypothesis that the onset of palatability-related population activity in GC marks a discrete shift in taste processing - the ensemble transition in taste-related firing that predicts behavior is in fact the emission of the decision to gape.
evidence: This is the interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The ensemble transition in taste-related firing that predicts behavior is in fact the emission of the decision to gape.
source: This result provides support for our overarching hypothesis that the onset of palatability-related population activity in GC marks a discrete shift in taste processing - the ensemble transition in taste-related firing that predicts behavior is in fact the emission of the decision to gape.
evidence: This is the interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Brief (0.5s) optogenetic perturbations of GC neurons impact the timing of the animal's decision to expel a bitter taste in the mouth, but only if those perturbations begin before the neural ensemble has shifted to palatability-related firing.
source: Here we show that GC neural ensemble dynamics described above are not merely 'efferent copy' reflections of processes occurring elsewhere, but are instead an indication of processing that is (to at least some extent, see below) intrinsic to GC. Brief (0.5s) optogenetic perturbations of GC neurons impact the timing of the animal's decision to expel a bitter taste in the mouth, but only if those perturbations begin before the neural ensemble has shifted to palatability-related firing.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding of the study.

claim: GC neural ensemble dynamics are not merely 'efferent copy' reflections of processes occurring elsewhere, but are instead an indication of processing that is intrinsic to GC.
source: Here we show that GC neural ensemble dynamics described above are not merely 'efferent copy' reflections of processes occurring elsewhere, but are instead an indication of processing that is (to at least some extent, see below) intrinsic to GC.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that perturbations of GC affect behavior.

claim: Cortical disruptions have no impact beyond the tipping point of the shift to palatability-related firing, as the control of the ongoing movements themselves shifts elsewhere.
source: Thus, a unique moment in time (the shift of population activity to reflect stimulus palatability), despite being enormously variable in latency from trial-to-trial, reflects a tipping point in taste processing; cortical disruptions have no impact beyond this tipping point, as the control of the ongoing movements themselves shifts elsewhere (presumably to brainstem pattern generators that control the ingestion-egestion mouth movements themselves in real time, see Travers et al., 1997; Travers et al., 2000).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of late perturbations on ongoing gaping.

claim: Control of ongoing gaping movements presumably shifts to brainstem pattern generators that control the ingestion-egestion mouth movements themselves in real time.
source: Thus, a unique moment in time (the shift of population activity to reflect stimulus palatability), despite being enormously variable in latency from trial-to-trial, reflects a tipping point in taste processing; cortical disruptions have no impact beyond this tipping point, as the control of the ongoing movements themselves shifts elsewhere (presumably to brainstem pattern generators that control the ingestion-egestion mouth movements themselves in real time, see Travers et al., 1997; Travers et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings and cited prior work.

claim: A massively interconnected network of forebrain regions underlies or reflects taste processing.
source: A massively interconnected network of forebrain regions underlies or reflects taste processing - in addition to GC, this network includes the central and basolateral nuclei of the amygdala (CeA and BLA, Nishijo et al., 1998; Grossman et al., 2008; Fontanini et al., 2009; Sadacca et al., 2012), hippocampus (Ho et al., 2011), lateral hypothalamus (LH, Yamamoto et al., 1989; Li et al., 2013), the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST, Norgren, 1976; Li and Cho, 2006), the parabrachial nuclei of the pons (Baez-Santiago et al., 2016), and the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS, Di Lorenzo and Lemon, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Several brain regions have been shown to integrate sensory and motor aspects of taste stimuli in their responses.
source: Several of these brain regions have been shown to integrate sensory and motor aspects of taste stimuli in their responses (Sadacca et al., 2016; Baez-Santiago et al., 2016; Denman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Multiple forebrain regions send direct descending feedback to the primary brainstem taste regions, influencing both their activity and generation of orofacial movements.
source: Furthermore, multiple forebrain regions send direct descending feedback to the primary brainstem taste regions, influencing both their activity (Di Lorenzo, 2000; Cho et al., 2003; Li et al., 2005) and generation of orofacial movements (Zhang and Sasamoto, 1990; Berridge and Valenstein, 1991; Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1992; Travers et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Rodents remain able to produce gapes following ablation of GC.
source: Given this widely distributed network of processing nodes, it is to be expected that perturbation (or disruption over long periods of time) of one (or a few) of the participatory nodes will initiate homeostatic mechanisms that minimize the resultant degradation of behavior; thus, it is unsurprising that rodents remain able to produce gapes following ablation (King et al., 2015) or extended disruption of GC (Li et al., 2016) - in fact, the basic gaping response to quinine is produced even in decerebrate rats (Grill and Norgren, 1978b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior lesion study.

claim: Rodents remain able to produce gapes following extended disruption of GC.
source: Given this widely distributed network of processing nodes, it is to be expected that perturbation (or disruption over long periods of time) of one (or a few) of the participatory nodes will initiate homeostatic mechanisms that minimize the resultant degradation of behavior; thus, it is unsurprising that rodents remain able to produce gapes following ablation (King et al., 2015) or extended disruption of GC (Li et al., 2016) - in fact, the basic gaping response to quinine is produced even in decerebrate rats (Grill and Norgren, 1978b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior optogenetic study.

claim: The basic gaping response to quinine is produced even in decerebrate rats.
source: Given this widely distributed network of processing nodes, it is to be expected that perturbation (or disruption over long periods of time) of one (or a few) of the participatory nodes will initiate homeostatic mechanisms that minimize the resultant degradation of behavior; thus, it is unsurprising that rodents remain able to produce gapes following ablation (King et al., 2015) or extended disruption of GC (Li et al., 2016) - in fact, the basic gaping response to quinine is produced even in decerebrate rats (Grill and Norgren, 1978b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior decerebration study.

claim: Brief perturbations of GC do significantly alter gaping behaviors.
source: Nonetheless, we find that brief perturbations of GC do significantly alter these behaviors (as do lesions of other areas, such as gustatory thalamus; Grill and Norgren, 1978b), proving that far more than the minimal circuit is involved in triggering them in situ.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding of the study.

claim: 2.5s long optogenetic perturbations delayed the onset of gaping even in control (no-laser) trials.
source: Lengthy disruptions of GC activity appear to have lasting effects that can confound the interpretation of their behavioral impact - our 2.5s long optogenetic perturbations delayed the onset of gaping even in control (no-laser) trials.
evidence: This is measured from the behavioral analysis of 2.5s perturbation sessions.

claim: Similar optogenetic protocols have been shown to have no observable impact on cell integrity in GC, even for perturbations much longer than 2.5s.
source: Such spillover effects may reflect cellular or network-level processes, but they cannot be attributed to cell death caused by the perturbation: in our case, similar optogenetic protocols have been shown to have no observable impact on cell integrity in GC, even for perturbations much longer than 2.5s (Maier et al., 2015; Flores et al., 2018); furthermore, the same rats in later sessions produced normally-timed orofacial responses on the control trials.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies using similar optogenetic protocols.

claim: Even early (pre-transition) GC perturbations delay gaping.
source: This conclusion is bolstered by findings showing that: (1) even early - that is pre-transition - GC perturbations delay gaping; and (2) palatability-related firing does not immediately return to normal levels following cessation of perturbation (as would be expected if GC was simply an output path reflecting processing performed elsewhere).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: Palatability-related firing does not immediately return to normal levels following cessation of perturbation.
source: This conclusion is bolstered by findings showing that: (1) even early - that is pre-transition - GC perturbations delay gaping; and (2) palatability-related firing does not immediately return to normal levels following cessation of perturbation (as would be expected if GC was simply an output path reflecting processing performed elsewhere).
evidence: This is shown in the palatability analysis in Figure 3.

claim: 0.5s perturbations reveal that GC contributes to the instigation of a gaping bout but plays no role in the maintenance of gaping once it begins.
source: Our 0.5s perturbations reveal that GC contributes to the instigation of a gaping bout but plays no role in the maintenance of gaping once it begins.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of early/middle vs. late perturbations on gaping.

claim: Modulatory signals propagate out of GC to influence the choice of a motor program in brainstem circuits, which is then implemented and controlled locally.
source: These data suggest a dynamic flow of processing control within the larger taste network: modulatory signals propagate out of GC (signals that likely develop under the guidance of basolateral amygdala; Piette et al., 2012) to influence the choice of a motor program in brainstem circuits, which is then implemented and controlled locally.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings and cited prior work.

claim: The proposed role of cortex in taste processing has deep similarities to the role of neuromodulatory systems in the circuits underlying Aplysia feeding.
source: At its heart, the proposed role of cortex in this model of taste processing has deep similarities to the role of neuromodulatory systems in the circuits underlying Aplysia feeding (Dacks and Weiss, 2013), leech swimming (Crisp and Mesce, 2004), control of gastric rhythms in the lobster and crab (Marder and Bucher, 2007), and rat whisking (Hattox et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a conceptual comparison supported by citations to prior work on other systems.

claim: The discreteness, coherence and inter-trial variability of the ensemble dynamics suggests that GC functions as an attractor network.
source: The discreteness, coherence and inter-trial variability of the ensemble dynamics suggests that GC functions as an attractor network in playing this role (Hopfield, 1982; Amit, 1992): (1) attractor networks with multiple quasi-stable states can reproduce the sudden switches of activity seen in GC ensembles (Miller and Katz, 2010); (2) the transition durations and state lifetime statistics of GC population dynamics are more in line with a dynamically switching attractor model than linear models of firing rate evolution (Jones et al., 2007; Sadacca et al., 2016); and (3) nonlinear attractor-based circuits that exploit the noise inherent in neural processing more optimally perform the decision to ingest or expel a taste, which rats need no training to perform, than do linear integrating circuits (Miller and Katz, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and cited theoretical work.

claim: Perturbations beginning 50ms after ensemble neural transitions to palatability-related firing have no impact on gaping.
source: Our data demonstrate that perturbations beginning 50ms after ensemble neural transitions to palatability-related firing have no impact on gaping.
evidence: This is measured from the trial-specific behavioral analysis.

claim: GC perturbation becomes ineffective at delaying gaping almost immediately following the transition.
source: While one could hypothesize reasons that perturbation beginning very soon after an ensemble transition should be effective in delaying gaping – the fact that transitions between quasi-stable states of GC processing, however sudden, cannot be instantaneous (time constants of neural firing ensure that there is some finite, albeit small amount of time across which the ensemble makes the 'jump' from one state of activity to another), for instance, and the fact that our change-point analysis technique provides only a noisy estimate of state transition times – our data and analyses suggest that GC perturbation becomes ineffective at delaying gaping almost immediately following the transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the trial-specific behavioral analysis.

claim: GC appears to emit a 'gape signal', after which it is no longer involved in the implementation of that signal.
source: GC appears to emit a 'gape signal', after which it is no longer involved in the implementation of that signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of perturbations after the transition.

claim: GC ensemble firing reflects the palatability of both appetitive and aversive tastes.
source: We consider this possibility highly unlikely, however, for several reasons: (1) GC ensemble firing reflects the palatability of both appetitive and aversive tastes (Figure 3, Katz et al., 2001; also see Fonseca et al., 2018), even if palatability is modified by learning (Moran and Katz, 2014); (2) the latency and inter-trial variability of the onset of palatability-related ensemble activity is similar for palatable and aversive tastes (Sadacca et al., 2016); (3) there is considerable overlap in the brainstem circuits that underlie the distinct palatability-related orofacial behaviors (Travers et al., 2000; Chen and Travers, 2003; Venugopal et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2014), resulting in similar latencies in the onset of these behaviors after taste delivery (Travers and Norgren, 1986); and (4) independent analysis has suggested that orofacial behaviors reflecting aversiveness and palatableness lie on a single parametric continuum (Breslin et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3 and citations to prior studies.

claim: The latency and inter-trial variability of the onset of palatability-related ensemble activity is similar for palatable and aversive tastes.
source: We consider this possibility highly unlikely, however, for several reasons: (1) GC ensemble firing reflects the palatability of both appetitive and aversive tastes (Figure 3, Katz et al., 2001; also see Fonseca et al., 2018), even if palatability is modified by learning (Moran and Katz, 2014); (2) the latency and inter-trial variability of the onset of palatability-related ensemble activity is similar for palatable and aversive tastes (Sadacca et al., 2016); (3) there is considerable overlap in the brainstem circuits that underlie the distinct palatability-related orofacial behaviors (Travers et al., 2000; Chen and Travers, 2003; Venugopal et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2014), resulting in similar latencies in the onset of these behaviors after taste delivery (Travers and Norgren, 1986); and (4) independent analysis has suggested that orofacial behaviors reflecting aversiveness and palatableness lie on a single parametric continuum (Breslin et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: There is considerable overlap in the brainstem circuits that underlie the distinct palatability-related orofacial behaviors.
source: We consider this possibility highly unlikely, however, for several reasons: (1) GC ensemble firing reflects the palatability of both appetitive and aversive tastes (Figure 3, Katz et al., 2001; also see Fonseca et al., 2018), even if palatability is modified by learning (Moran and Katz, 2014); (2) the latency and inter-trial variability of the onset of palatability-related ensemble activity is similar for palatable and aversive tastes (Sadacca et al., 2016); (3) there is considerable overlap in the brainstem circuits that underlie the distinct palatability-related orofacial behaviors (Travers et al., 2000; Chen and Travers, 2003; Venugopal et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2014), resulting in similar latencies in the onset of these behaviors after taste delivery (Travers and Norgren, 1986); and (4) independent analysis has suggested that orofacial behaviors reflecting aversiveness and palatableness lie on a single parametric continuum (Breslin et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Orofacial behaviors reflecting aversiveness and palatableness lie on a single parametric continuum.
source: We consider this possibility highly unlikely, however, for several reasons: (1) GC ensemble firing reflects the palatability of both appetitive and aversive tastes (Figure 3, Katz et al., 2001; also see Fonseca et al., 2018), even if palatability is modified by learning (Moran and Katz, 2014); (2) the latency and inter-trial variability of the onset of palatability-related ensemble activity is similar for palatable and aversive tastes (Sadacca et al., 2016); (3) there is considerable overlap in the brainstem circuits that underlie the distinct palatability-related orofacial behaviors (Travers et al., 2000; Chen and Travers, 2003; Venugopal et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2014), resulting in similar latencies in the onset of these behaviors after taste delivery (Travers and Norgren, 1986); and (4) independent analysis has suggested that orofacial behaviors reflecting aversiveness and palatableness lie on a single parametric continuum (Breslin et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior behavioral analysis.

claim: The transition of GC population activity to reflect stimulus palatability marks a shift in processing control, irrespective of the palatability of the tastant.
source: These lines of evidence are consistent with the suggestion that cortex plays similar roles in the initiation of acceptance and rejection behaviors, which leads us to speculate that the transition of GC population activity to reflect stimulus palatability marks a shift in processing control, irrespective of the palatability of the tastant.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings and cited prior work.

claim: The results demonstrate a dynamic role for cortex in the processing of tastes.
source: In summary, the balance of our results demonstrate a dynamic role for cortex in the processing of tastes; because this role involves ensemble activity states with variable trial-to-trial latencies, it cannot be discerned using standard analyses that average across trials – trial-specific analyses, such as those underlying the results in Figure 7, supersede across-trial analyses such as those described in Figure 3.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Trial-specific analyses supersede across-trial analyses for understanding the role of cortex in taste processing.
source: In summary, the balance of our results demonstrate a dynamic role for cortex in the processing of tastes; because this role involves ensemble activity states with variable trial-to-trial latencies, it cannot be discerned using standard analyses that average across trials – trial-specific analyses, such as those underlying the results in Figure 7, supersede across-trial analyses such as those described in Figure 3.
evidence: This methodological point is demonstrated by comparing the results in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: The results reveal the importance of a unique moment in time that denotes a reliable shift of processing control.
source: They reveal the importance of a unique moment in time that, despite being massively variable in latency from trial to trial, denotes a reliable shift of processing control - a modulatory signal emerging (at least partly) from cortical circuits that is passed (presumably) to a brainstem central pattern generator.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: A modulatory signal emerges at least partly from cortical circuits and is passed presumably to a brainstem central pattern generator.
source: They reveal the importance of a unique moment in time that, despite being massively variable in latency from trial to trial, denotes a reliable shift of processing control - a modulatory signal emerging (at least partly) from cortical circuits that is passed (presumably) to a brainstem central pattern generator.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The results suggest an attractor-like network of activity, potentially spread across interconnected brain regions, underlying the animal's decision to ingest or expel the tastant in the mouth.
source: These results suggest an attractor-like network of activity (although they could also be consistent with networks with thresholds), potentially spread across interconnected brain regions, underlying the animal's decision to ingest or expel the tastant in the mouth - perturbations to this network can disrupt its functioning transiently, but only if it has not yet settled into the final, behaviorally-relevant stable state.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Perturbations to the taste processing network can disrupt its functioning transiently, but only if it has not yet settled into the final, behaviorally-relevant stable state.
source: These results suggest an attractor-like network of activity (although they could also be consistent with networks with thresholds), potentially spread across interconnected brain regions, underlying the animal's decision to ingest or expel the tastant in the mouth - perturbations to this network can disrupt its functioning transiently, but only if it has not yet settled into the final, behaviorally-relevant stable state.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding of the study.

claim: Adult, female Long-Evans rats (n = 5) served as subjects in the study.
source: Adult, female Long-Evans rats (n = 5; 275–300g at time of virus injection; 300–350g at time of electrode implantation) served as subjects in our study (in our hands, female Long-Evans rats have proven more docile than males, but we have observed no sex differences in the basic cortical dynamics of taste responding).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental subjects.

claim: AAV9 coding for ArchT and green fluorescent protein was injected into GC.
source: We injected adeno-associated virus (AAV9) coding for ArchT and green fluorescent protein (AAV9-CAG-ArchT-GFP, 2.5 × 1011 particles per mL) into GC.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental methods.

claim: This AAV serotype has been shown to effectively spread to and infect all cell types.
source: This AAV serotype has been shown to effectively spread to and infect all cell types (Aschauer et al., 2013) in regions including GC (Maier et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: Rats received intra-oral deliveries of 30mM sucrose (Dil Suc), 300mM sucrose (Conc Suc), 0.1mM Quinine-HCl (Dil Qui) and 1mM Quinine-HCl (Conc Qui).
source: The rats received intra-oral deliveries of 30mM sucrose (Dil Suc), 300mM sucrose (Conc Suc), 0.1mM Quinine-HCl (Dil Qui) and 1mM Quinine-HCl (Conc Qui).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental stimuli.

claim: A 532 nm, DPSS laser was used for all optogenetic perturbations.
source: We used a 532 nm, DPSS laser (Laserglow Technologies), connected to the implanted ferrules using standard FC/PC patch cables (Thorlabs), for all optogenetic perturbations.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental methods.

claim: The strength of the laser input was calibrated to yield an illumination power of 40mW at the tip of the optical fiber.
source: The strength of the laser input was calibrated, prior to opto-trode implantation, to yield an illumination power of 40mW at the tip of the optical fiber.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental methods.

claim: This output power perturbs all ArchT infected neurons in a 1mm3 sphere below the tip of the fiber in vivo.
source: This output power perturbs all ArchT infected neurons in a 1mm3 sphere below the tip of the fiber in vivo (Han et al., 2011; Yizhar et al., 2011) - a sphere that encompasses about 33% of GC in the caudal-rostral axis (Kosar et al., 1986; Maier et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior optogenetic characterization studies.

claim: These parameters have previously been shown to reduce the activity of ArchT+ cortical neurons with minimal latency and damage.
source: These parameters have previously been shown to reduce the activity of ArchT+ cortical neurons with minimal latency and damage (Maier et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Flores et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies using similar optogenetic protocols.
